Create Voronoi polygons from points with CRS handling and optional clipping

Source: R/tessellation.R
create_voronoi_polygons.Rd

Assigns every location in the study area to its nearest input point, giving one cell per point. This is the tessellation to reach for when the observations themselves define the regions of interest (sampling sites, monitoring stations, service points), because cell size then adapts to sampling density instead of being imposed by a fixed grid: dense areas get small cells and sparse areas large ones. Prefer create_grid_polygons() instead when you need equal-area cells or a resolution independent of where the data happen to be.

Usage

create_voronoi_polygons(
  points_sf,
  boundary = NULL,
  expand = 0,
  clip = TRUE,
  keep_duplicates = FALSE,
  crs = NULL,
  quiet = FALSE,
  cover = NULL
)

Arguments

points_sf

An sf object with POINT/MULTIPOINT geometries. Points with no CRS whose coordinates look like lon/lat (the heuristic ensure_projected() applies, with its warning) are taken as EPSG:4326 and projected, as lon/lat points are.

boundary

Optional polygonal sf object. When exactly one of points_sf and boundary has a CRS, the other is interpreted in it, with a warning. CRS-less points, and a CRS-less boundary given with projected points, are read as harmonize_crs() does (lon/lat-looking coordinates are reprojected from EPSG:4326, others are stamped); CRS-less points that do not look like lon/lat cannot take a geographic boundary's CRS, and are refused with an error. A CRS-less boundary given with lon/lat points (or with CRS-less points taken as lon/lat) is read as lon/lat when its coordinates fit the lon/lat envelope, and refused with an error otherwise.

expand

Numeric; absolute distance, in the working CRS's units, by which the boundary (or the hull derived from the points) is grown before the diagram is built. With clip = TRUE the cells are clipped to the grown boundary, so they reach expand beyond the study area, and a point up to expand outside it gets a cell and an index value. The grown boundary is the one returned as boundary.

clip

Logical; intersect cells with boundary.

keep_duplicates

Logical. Has no effect on the result: coincident points are merged before the diagram is built either way, so they share one cell and all of them are indexed to it.

crs

Optional target CRS: anything sf::st_crs() accepts, including an sf or sfc layer, whose CRS is used. A projected CRS is the working CRS. A geographic one (EPSG:4326, say) is the CRS the result is returned in: the cells are built in the local projected CRS ensure_projected() picks for the points, so they are nearest-point cells on the ground, and are then transformed, with long edges densified. Seeds that are the centres a profile scored are built in the CRS the profile worked in instead (see "Seeds a profile scored").

quiet

Logical; suppress this function's progress message()s. It does not silence R warnings, nor the package's console log echo (see spatialkit_quiet for that). Default FALSE.

cover

Optional sf or sfc layer the cells have to hold, read when there is no boundary: the observations (points), or a polygon. The boundary is then derived from it instead of from points_sf: the convex hull of the cover's points, or its polygons, grown by 2 percent of the diagonal. This is what seeds need, because seeds lie inside the data they stand for and their own hull stops short of it (see "Details"). When NULL, the cover the seeding functions attach is used (attr(points_sf, "cover"), set by get_voronoi_seeds(), voronoi_seeds_kmeans() and voronoi_seeds_random()). A cover with no CRS is read in the coordinates of points_sf, and one in another CRS is transformed. A generator outside the cover keeps its ground (the hull of the generators is added); a cover that holds none of the generators is set aside with a warning. With a boundary, the boundary sets the cells and cover is only checked against them: the number of its points that fall outside every cell is returned as params$cover_outside, with a warning of class "spatialkit_unassigned" when it is not 0 (a polygon cover is not checked).

Value

A list with cells, index, boundary, method and params. index holds one cell_id per row of points_sf, and NA for a point that falls outside every cell, which means outside the study area (grown by expand when it is positive), so a summary built from it counts only the points the tessellation actually covers. Such points are counted in params$n_outside, and a warning of class "spatialkit_unassigned" gives their number. boundary is the boundary the cells were built in: the one supplied or derived, grown by expand. params$boundary_source says where it came from: "boundary" (the argument), "cover" (the cover argument), "seeds' cover" (the cover attached to points_sf) or "points" (the hull of points_sf itself). params$cover_outside is the number of cover points outside every cell when a point cover was given with a boundary, and NULL otherwise. params$partition is present when points_sf is a layer of seeds that records the kind of partition that placed it (attr(points_sf, "partition"), see get_voronoi_seeds()): the same list, so the cells say what built them. Seeds of plain k-means record nothing, and params then has no such element; neither has it for points that are not seeds. params$count_rule is present when points_sf carries the record of how its count was set (attr(points_sf, "count_rule"): the seeds of a select_resolution() result, or seeds a seeding function placed from one): the same list, which the cells carry too as attr(cells, "count_rule"). assign_features_to_polygons() copies it to the rows it assigns, and summarize_by_cell() checks its result against it.

Details

The heavy lifting is sf::st_voronoi(). What this adds is the surrounding bookkeeping: projecting lon/lat input, building and buffering an envelope so edge cells are bounded, clipping to boundary, restoring the point-to-cell correspondence that st_voronoi() scrambles, and stamping stable cell_id values.

The generators are the points' vertices, not the features. A MULTIPOINT feature with several vertices therefore gets one cell per vertex, and its index entry is the smallest cell_id among the cells it touches; the others are referenced by no feature. Other functions in the package (prep_model_data(), make_folds()) reduce such a feature to its centroid instead, so cast to POINT, or take centroids, first if one cell per feature is what you want.

With no boundary the cells are clipped to a boundary derived from the data. For observations that is their own convex hull grown by 2 percent of its diagonal, so every observation has a cell. Seeds are different: k-means centres, random points in a study area and the centres a resolution profile scored all lie inside the ground they stand for, and cells clipped to the hull of the seeds leave the edge of that ground uncovered (on 3,000 uniform points, 72 percent of them at 4 seeds, 25 percent at 25 and 4 percent at 100). The boundary is therefore derived from the cover when there is one: the argument, or the cover the seeding functions attach to their result. A layer that looks like seeds and has neither a boundary nor a cover (seeds bound with rbind(), which drops the attribute, or built by hand) gets the seeds' own hull and a warning of class "spatialkit_no_cover".

Seeds a profile scored

The seeds of a select_resolution() result, and the seeds get_voronoi_seeds() or voronoi_seeds_kmeans() return for one, are the centres resolution_profile() scored, and their record of the count (attr(, "count_rule")) says so (scored_cells = TRUE) and holds the centres in the CRS the profile worked in. Unless a projected crs is given, their cells are built in that CRS, whatever CRS the seeds arrive in (degrees, or the CRS of a boundary they were placed in), and returned in it, or in a geographic crs when one is given. When the seeds are those centres (as many, each at a different centre, within a thousandth of its distance from the next nearest), each is first put at its centre as the record holds it, so rounding the seeds took on in another CRS does not move an edge. The cells are then the cells each row was scored in, and assign_features_to_polygons() gives a point on an edge between two of them the cell the profile scored it in.

See also

Other tessellation: build_tessellation(), create_grid_polygons(), create_grid_polygons_cached(), ensure_stable_poly_id(), get_voronoi_seeds(), plot_tessellation_map(), voronoi_seeds_kmeans(), voronoi_seeds_random()

Examples

library(sf)
set.seed(1)
pts <- st_as_sf(
  data.frame(x = 5e5 + runif(15, 0, 100), y = 5e6 + runif(15, 0, 100)),
  coords = c("x", "y"), crs = 32632
)
res <- create_voronoi_polygons(pts, quiet = TRUE)
res$cells   # one polygon per unique point, with stable cell_id
#> Simple feature collection with 15 features and 1 field
#> Geometry type: POLYGON
#> Dimension:     XY
#> Bounding box:  xmin: 500003.5 ymin: 4999999 xmax: 500097.1 ymax: 5000102
#> Projected CRS: WGS 84 / UTM zone 32N
#> First 10 features:
#>                          geometry cell_id
#> 1  POLYGON ((500024.2 5000020,...       1
#> 2  POLYGON ((500030.5 5000080,...       2
#> 3  POLYGON ((500007.1 5000040,...       3
#> 4  POLYGON ((500024.2 5000020,...       4
#> 5  POLYGON ((500048.1 5000053,...       5
#> 6  POLYGON ((500025 5000064, 5...       6
#> 7  POLYGON ((500055.9 5000081,...       7
#> 8  POLYGON ((500037.4 5000019,...       8
#> 9  POLYGON ((500071.5 5000085,...       9
#> 10 POLYGON ((500044.6 5000033,...      10
res$index   # cell_id assignment for each input point
